components.title: Recap of Protocol Lifecycles and Core Primitives
components.teaches: Summarize the JSON-RPC initialization handshake and introduce the three core MCP primitives: resources, prompts, and tools. Students will distinguish between passive data provision (resources) and dynamic model operations (tools).

components.title: Defining Resources and Resource Templates in Context Schemas
components.teaches: Explain how context servers expose data via URI schemes and parameterized resource templates. Students will identify the schema fields used to define static text/binary content, MIME types, and dynamic URI-based subscription updates.

components.title: Tool Definitions and Dynamic Execution Callbacks
components.teaches: Examine how servers declare executable tools using JSON Schema for input argument validation. Students will follow the flow from tool discovery (`tools/list`) through host invocation (`tools/call`) to returning structured execution results or errors.

components.title: Developer Workspace Configuration Schemas and Server Registration
components.teaches: Break down the structure of workspace configuration files, such as `mcpServers` sections in desktop or IDE configuration files. Students will identify mandatory fields including command, args, env variables, and transport settings required to launch context servers.

components.title: Security Boundaries, Environment Isolation, and Access Control
components.teaches: Analyze security risks associated with granting language models access to local files and CLI execution via context protocols. Students will identify mitigation strategies, including sandboxed subprocess execution, prompt injection defense in tool outputs, and explicit user-in-the-loop approvals.

components.title: Inspecting Configuration Templates for Model Context Protocols
components.teaches: Walk through a supplied developer workspace template to identify configured context servers, missing schema fields, and transport definitions. Students will pinpoint configuration discrepancies such as misconfigured PATHs, missing environment variables, or schema type mismatches.

components.title: Diagnosing Protocol Connection Failures and Logging Workflows
components.teaches: Demonstrate how to detect and trace common protocol runtime errors using client diagnostic logs and server error codes. Students will evaluate stderr streams, malformed JSON-RPC payloads, and unhandled transport disconnects.

video.description:
This video contains a very simple explanation of MCP, also known as Model Context Protocol. We will first understand what exactly is MCP and how it easing up the development of AI applications and then we will go into the technical details of how the actual protocol looks like. We will look into the code of MCP client and Server both.

Sample MCP client: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk/blob/main/examples/clients/simple-chatbot/mcp_simple_chatbot/main.py
Google maps MCP server: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/blob/main/src/google-maps/index.ts#L297
MCP Schema: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/specification/blob/main/schema/2024-11-05/schema.ts

video.description:
Google MCPs → https://goo.gle/3PYkjky 
Build an ADK agent with Google MCPs → https://goo.gle/4o6h8DP 
Connect an MCP server to an AI agent → https://goo.gle/4uk7YW2 

APIs were built for deterministic programs, but AI models reason probabilistically. So how do you get your AI agents to talk to your tools and data without writing messy, custom integration code every time? Enter the Model Context Protocol (MCP). In this video, Smitha Kolan explains what MCP is, how it standardizes the way AI models discover and interact with external resources, and why it's becoming the new standard over traditional APIs for AI-powered applications
